extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers / coffee‑house public interested in manners, marriage, and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic periodical essays offering moral and social advice about behaviour, marriage, fashion, and public life—aimed at a general educated readership and often mixing anecdote, satire, and practical counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical or romantic style when making love
rubrics_metrics.description: We generally make Love in a Style, and with Sentiments very unfit for ordinary Life: They are half Theatrical, half Romantick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals and expectations of love should be realistic rather than exaggerated; theatrical/romantic sentiment inflates expectations and leads to disappointment in ordinary married life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reason with passion in marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: He who brings his Reason to support his Passion... will form himself accordingly, and adapt his Mind to the Nature of his Circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A husband should temper desire with practical consideration (duty, honour, friendship) so he can accept responsibilities (father, steward, advocate) and not be thrown by ordinary domestic hardships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect human frailty in a spouse
rubrics_metrics.description: Beholds what he loves as liable to all the Calamities of human Life both in Body and Mind... and even at the best what must bring upon him new Cares and new Relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipating age, sickness, impatience, or sullenness in a partner reduces resentment and fosters patience; judging a spouse only by idealized charms invites indifference and anger when desire flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a disposition to be pleased
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a Rule... to preserve always a Disposition to be pleased. This cannot be supported but by considering things in their right light, and as Nature has form'd them, and not as our own Fancies or Appetites would have them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an outlook that finds pleasure in small, ordinary occurrences (children's sayings, household moments); this temperament yields greater domestic happiness and resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value shared domestic joys and consolations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something in it that doubles Satisfactions, because others participate them; and dispels Afflictions, because others are exempt from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Married life intensifies pleasures and mitigates sorrows through shared experience—this communal aspect is a key virtue of the married condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patience and temper rather than corporal correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are visited with Women of Spirit... I should rather recommend... to form themselves for the World by Patience at home. Socrates... own'd that he ow'd great part of his Virtue to the Exercise which his useful Wife constantly gave it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endurance, wit, and self-improvement are preferable to blows; physical correction, if used, ought to be rare (used sparingly) and is not the recommended response to difficult spouses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't interpret neighbours' misfortunes as divine punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot be guilty of a greater Act of Uncharitableness, than to interpret the Afflictions which befal our Neighbours, as Punishments and Judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious sentiment should incline to compassion and mild constructions of events; turning every misfortune into a moral judgment aggravates suffering and corrodes charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive diffidence that hinders advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of low Fortunes and great Modesty... what wrong Measures their Diffidence of themselves, and Fear of offending, often obliges them to take; and what a Pity it is that their greatest Virtues and Qualities... are the main Obstacle in the way of their Preferment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While modesty is a virtue, excessive timidity or silence can prevent meritorious people from gaining opportunities; a balance of humility and assertiveness is advised for social/professional advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place honour in conscious well‑doing, not outward titles
rubrics_metrics.description: All the Words of Lordship, Honour, and Grace, are only Repetitions to a Man that the King has order'd him to be called so; but no Evidences that there is any thing in himself that would give the Man... those Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctions are truly valuable only insofar as they enable public action; internal conscience and reflection on worthy actions are a more solid source of honour than external appellations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character sketches: use domestic detail and comic types
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters such as the Hen‑peck'd, the Cot‑Quean (a husband who 'wears the Petticoat'), and other comic domestic portraits are offered with concrete household details (cooking, preserving, fussiness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective periodical satire and humour use vivid, specific domestic particulars and recognizable social types to expose folly and entertain readers; contrast and anecdote sharpen the portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for directors of a fashionable society (satirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Old Beaus are to be presented in the first place... it will... be absolutely necessary to take in all Time‑Servers... such as, without any Conviction of Conscience or View of Interest, change with the World... Those who are in Fashion without apparent Merit, must be supposed to have latent Qualities... are to be regarded in forming these Lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the mock proposal for a Board of Directors of fashion, the suggested qualifications are satirical: include old beaus, time‑servers, obsequious followers, those who follow leaders for want of courage, and fashionable people lacking clear merit (assumed latent qualities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use common‑sense judgments alongside high politics
rubrics_metrics.description: A Porter's Decision... (in a play) and the coffee‑house debate show that ordinary people apply proverbs and practical solutions to seemingly great controversies (e.g., the dispute between Rechteren and Ménager reduced to lackey quarrel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or commenting on public affairs, juxtapose high political stakes with commonsense or popular perspectives to reveal absurdity or to humanize complex disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make epistolary personae speak with proper social station and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters reproduced (e.g., 'Monsieur Chezluy to Pharamond') are written to reflect the writer's station, modesty, and rhetorical aims—confessing modesty, refusing honours, and presenting reasons politely yet candidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using letters or fictional correspondents as devices, adjust diction, humility, and reasoning to match their social position and to advance rhetorical effect (persuasion, satire, exemplification).
